idiom

ID-ee-um -- three syllables, stress on the first syllable, ID. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Idiom is a phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from its individual words.

Her article used the idiom 'the ball is in your court' to describe the stalled treaty talks.

Example

'Stop pulling my leg!' Dad laughs at the dinner table. Six-year-old Leo ducks under the table to check, then pops back up, baffled: 'Nobody is touching your leg.' His sister explains that Dad means 'stop teasing me' -- the phrase has nothing to do with legs at all.

'Pulling my leg' is an idiom: a phrase whose real meaning -- teasing someone -- cannot be figured out from the individual words, which is exactly why literal-minded Leo checked under the table. Idioms have to be learned as whole chunks; no dictionary definition of 'pull' or 'leg' will ever add up to 'tease.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

figure of speech: A figure of speech is wording that is not meant literally but can be decoded on the spot -- call a defense 'a brick wall' and any listener works out the meaning. An idiom resists that decoding entirely: its meaning must be learned, because the words alone will never yield it.

turn of phrase: A turn of phrase is one speaker's own memorable way of putting a thought -- praise for personal style, coined in the moment. An idiom belongs to nobody in particular: it is a fixed phrase the whole language community shares, and its meaning cannot be built from its words.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

literal language: wording that means exactly what it says

plain statement: a direct remark with no hidden meaning

Where it sits · how far from literal the words drift — expression → idiom → inside joke

expression vs. idiom: Expression is a far milder label than idiom: any set phrase people use counts as an expression, even a perfectly literal one like 'have a seat' -- no drift from the words' plain meaning is required at all.

inside joke vs. idiom: An inside joke drifts even further from the literal words than an idiom does: an idiom's hidden meaning is at least public -- dictionaries list it -- but an inside joke's words mean nothing to anyone outside the small group that lived the story behind them.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — idio-

root — idio-: one's own, private, peculiar (Greek idios)

suffix — -om

suffix — -om: a thing formed; a result (Greek -oma)

Put it together

Put it together: Idiom comes from Greek idios, 'one's own, private' -- an idioma was a peculiarity, a way of speaking that belonged privately to one language or people. That is still the heart of the word: 'kick the bucket' belongs to English alone, and translating it word for word into any other language produces only confusion, because an idiom is a language's private property.

Use the root in a new word: idiosyncrasy

Use the root in a new word: idiosyncrasy: Wearing sandals in the snow was just one of the professor's idiosyncrasies.

Root Check

Word Choice

An idiom is always figurative and always fixed: 'kick the bucket' means to die, and you cannot reorder it to 'kick the pail' without breaking it. That fixedness is the test -- if the phrase means exactly what its words say ('close the door'), it is not an idiom. Idioms are the hardest part of any new language precisely because they must be learned whole, one chunk at a time.
